items.prompt: Which evidence most directly supports a bottom-up tabulation of a recurrence?
constraints: The same state meaning and transition will be used in every implementation.

options.text: Some recursive calls repeat, even though state bounds and dependency direction are still unknown.
The input is stored in an array.
The reachable states form a finite acyclic dependency graph whose bases and topological order are known.

feedback.reason: Bottom-up evaluation needs an explicit finite state domain and an order consistent with its dependencies.

blocks.text: Tabulation replaces demand-driven recursion with a planned traversal of states. To do that safely, the implementation must know which states exist, which values seed the computation, and which dependencies must precede each state. Overlap can motivate reuse but does not by itself provide those pieces. The same criterion applies whether the table is one-dimensional or multidimensional.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.overlap_only: Repetition suggests reuse, but tabulation also needs a well-defined state domain and an order that does not read unresolved states.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.array_input: Input representation does not determine whether the recurrence can be safely or usefully tabulated.

items.prompt: A recurrence is defined on dp(i, c), where i ranges from 0 to n and c from 0 to capacity. What is the safest initial tabulation shape?
constraints: No compression proof has been made.
Both i and c vary independently.

options.text: An array indexed only by c because capacity is the optimization constraint.
A table covering every reachable (i, c) pair, including terminal boundaries.
An array indexed only by i because DP tables should follow input positions.

feedback.reason: The uncompressed table should represent the full state pair so each cell has one unambiguous meaning.

blocks.text: A table cell is a materialized state result. Because both i and c distinguish future behavior, the direct representation has one axis for each. A later proof may make the item layer implicit and compress storage, but beginning with a one-axis table would mix semantic states before dependencies and update order are understood. Include terminal rows or columns that the transition reads.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index_only: Different capacities at the same item index can have different feasible choices and values, so they cannot share one cell.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.capacity_only: Without a proven layer schedule or compression, the table would lose which item suffix or prefix the value represents.

items.prompt: A bottom-up alignment table has (m + 1)(n + 1) cells and performs O(1) work per cell. Select its time and table space.
constraints: Input strings are not counted as extra space.

feedback.reason: There are Θ(mn) cells and each is computed once with constant transition work.

blocks.text: The extra boundary row and column do not change the Θ(mn) state count. Visiting each cell once gives O(mn) time, and retaining every cell gives O(mn) extra space. A memoized version has the same worst-case bound when all pairs are reachable. Tabulation may still be faster in practice through contiguous access and no recursive calls, while row compression can reduce space only after a dependency proof.

items.prompt: Order the core stages of a bottom-up DP computation.
constraints: The state, transition, and dependency direction are already defined.

elements.text: Allocate the complete state domain, including boundary states.
Initialize every base and impossible-state sentinel.
Evaluate nonterminal states in a dependency-safe order.
Read the state that represents the original problem.

feedback.reason: Tabulation is valid only when semantic seeds precede dependent states and the answer is read after all of its dependencies are resolved.

blocks.text: Every table phase establishes the next phase’s inputs

items: Allocate the complete semantic state domain, including every terminal row, column or index the recurrence can read.
Initialize base states and impossible-state sentinels explicitly instead of accepting storage defaults.
Evaluate nonterminal states in a topological order of the recurrence dependencies.
Extract the state representing the original problem only after all of its prerequisites are complete.

blocks.text: Reading the answer before the fill returns a default or partial value; filling before semantic seeds propagates invalid inputs. The lifecycle follows dependency readiness rather than allocation convenience.

blocks.title: Bottom-up lifecycle
blocks.text: Allocate domain → seed bases and sentinels → fill in dependency order → extract the answer.

items.prompt: What is the strongest way to justify replacing a full grid DP table with one row?
constraints: The full recurrence is already correct.
Only the final value is required.

options.text: Prove every one-row read represents the same logical predecessor as in the full table.
Show both versions have O(rows × columns) time and return the same kind of result.
Use one row because that optimization is common for grid recurrences with neighboring dependencies.

feedback.reason: Correctness depends on preserving the logical version of every dependency, not on matching asymptotic time or a common pattern.

blocks.text: The full table provides an unambiguous reference: each transition names exact predecessor cells. A rolling implementation must map every array read to those same logical values at the moment it occurs. This proof exposes whether update order overwrites a needed predecessor. Complexity and convention are secondary; semantic read equivalence is decisive.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_big_o_time: Equal time complexity does not prove that in-place reads refer to the correct logical layer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_row_common: A familiar optimization is not a proof; diagonal, multi-row, or reconstruction dependencies can invalidate it.

items.prompt: A minimum-cost table contains states that may be unreachable. Valid costs are nonnegative. How should unreachable cells be initialized?
constraints: A reachable base is initialized separately.

options.text: Use 0 because newly allocated numeric arrays start at zero.
Use -infinity so the sentinel is clearly special.
Use +infinity or an explicit unreachable marker so an unreachable state cannot win a minimum.

feedback.reason: For minimization, unreachable states must be worse than every valid cost, so +infinity or explicit reachability is safe.

blocks.text: A table default participates in transitions unless guarded. Zero is a legitimate low cost and can be selected as if an impossible predecessor were feasible. Positive infinity is dominated by any finite reachable cost and propagates impossibility until a valid transition reaches the state. For maximization the safe polarity is typically negative infinity; counting often uses zero ways.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Zero would look better than every positive valid cost and create paths that do not exist.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_infinity: Negative infinity would always win a minimum and contaminate every dependent state.

items.prompt: Every grid cell is open. A path-count table uses dp[r][c] = dp[r - 1][c] + dp[r][c - 1] for interior cells. Which bottom-up plan is correct?
constraints: Moves are only right and down.

options.text: Fill from bottom-right to top-left using the same predecessor formula.
Seed the origin, initialize or guard the first row and first column, then fill interior cells from top-left toward bottom-right.
Fill interior cells first and initialize the first row and column afterward.

feedback.reason: The recurrence's predecessors lie above and left, so boundaries must exist first and traversal must move toward their dependents.

blocks.text: The origin is the seed; cells on the first row or column have only one possible predecessor and need a boundary rule or an explicit guard. Once those values are valid, row-major traversal from top-left ensures both predecessors of every interior cell are available. A reverse traversal could work only with a reformulated recurrence using down and right successors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.interior_first: Interior cells read those boundary values, so computing them first consumes unresolved data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reverse_without_recurrence_change: That order reads cells above and left that have not yet been computed under the stated formulation.

items.prompt: What is the first design artifact to derive before writing nested loops for a bottom-up DP?

options.text: The state meaning and dependency graph, from which table boundaries and a safe evaluation order follow.
A forward loop template copied from another DP, regardless of this recurrence.
The final output formatting, because it determines which cells are legal to compute.
A table filled in arbitrary order, followed by a correction pass.

feedback.reason: Tabulation is a schedule over state dependencies; loops are an implementation of that schedule, not its source.

blocks.text: Write what each cell means, which predecessor cells the transition reads, and which base cells are known. Then choose row/column directions that ensure each predecessor is ready. Copying loop shape without this graph can read uninitialized or overwritten data.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.loop_direction_guess: The right direction changes with the recurrence and state formulation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_format_only: Output shape does not tell which internal dependencies must be computed first.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_table: A later correction cannot generally recover values computed from unavailable predecessors.

items.prompt: A two-dimensional table has independent base semantics on its first row and first column. What should initialization do before interior transitions run?

options.text: Fill the base row and column according to their state meanings, then compute interior cells from ready predecessors.
Fill the whole table with zero because every recurrence will overwrite it.
Compute interior cells first and infer boundary values from whichever neighbors are present.
Initialize only the destination because all other values are derived from it.

feedback.reason: Boundary states are the base cases of the two-dimensional recurrence and must carry their own semantic values.

blocks.text: For alignment, the first row/column may count insertions; for grid paths, they encode reachability and obstacles. Interior cells depend on these boundary values, so default zeros are correct only where the state meaning says so. Initialization must precede consumers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zeros_everywhere: A zero default may conflate unreachable, empty, and zero-cost states.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.interior_first: Interior transitions would read uninitialized boundary predecessors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.destination_only: The transition direction determines which bases are available; one endpoint is not a universal base.

items.prompt: A bottom-up DP fills every cell but the product requests only the final value. Which conclusion is valid about table storage?

options.text: Consider rolling rows or another compression only after verifying dependency liveness and whether reconstruction is required.
A final scalar always requires retaining every cell until return.
Keep only one cell because intermediate states are never part of the output.
Discard base states immediately because later cells no longer need them.

feedback.reason: Output requirements permit compression only when the transition's live predecessors and any witness needs remain satisfied.

blocks.text: A full table is simple and often useful as a reference. If each row depends only on bounded prior rows and only the value is needed, rolling storage can reduce space. Reconstruction, tie policies, or long-range dependencies may require additional information; output cardinality alone does not decide.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_full_table: Full storage is safe but not always necessary when dependencies are local and no witness is requested.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_cell_anyway: A recurrence may need multiple predecessor values at once.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.drop_bases: A base value may remain a live predecessor for later states or boundary transitions.

items.prompt: How should bottom-up tabulation choose its loop order?

options.text: Compute every dependency before the state that reads it.
Always use row-major order.
Always fill backward.
Any order works.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

items.prompt: Why are zero-capacity rows or empty-prefix columns common DP bases?

options.text: They represent an empty subproblem and anchor interior transitions.
They are arbitrary padding.
Every objective uses zero.
They store the final answer.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

items.prompt: Why can loop direction change an in-place capacity DP result?

options.text: Ascending versus descending order determines whether an item is reused in the same iteration.
Direction affects only speed.
Ascending is universally correct.
One row equals two rows in every order.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

items.prompt: What must be checked when a tabulated DP dimension has size zero?

options.text: Define the zero-size result and safe boundary initialization before neighboring cells are accessed.
Force a dimension to one and treat synthetic data as input.
Zero loop iterations automatically define the answer.
Fill absent dimensions with zeros.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.force: Synthetic states can change the result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip: Final access can still be invalid.
